2026-1.title: Verbosity : Brevity :: Insolence : ?
testing: Preserving the semantic relationship between two word pairs
2026-1.intuition: Do not begin by comparing spelling. First name the relationship in the completed pair: verbosity means excessive wordiness, while brevity means concise expression, so the two words are opposites. The missing word must therefore be the opposite of insolence. Insolence means rude or disrespectful behavior, so the required word is respect.

examApproach.heading: Label the first relationship
examApproach.body: Verbosity and brevity are antonyms: excessive use of words versus concise use of words.

examApproach.heading: Transfer exactly the same relationship
examApproach.body: The answer must be an antonym of insolence. Insolence means disrespect or impudence; its opposite is respect.

examApproach.heading: Stop once the semantic match is exact
examApproach.body: Option (B) is the only choice that preserves both the relationship type and direction.

steps.heading: Define the first word pair
steps.body: Verbosity is the quality of using more words than necessary. Brevity is shortness or conciseness. Hence the first pair expresses opposition.

steps.heading: Define the target word
steps.body: Insolence means rude disrespect, impudence, or lack of proper regard for another person.

steps.heading: Find the required opposite
steps.body: The opposite behavior is respect: showing due regard or consideration.

steps.heading: Complete the analogy
steps.body: Both sides now use the same antonym relationship in the same direction.

elimination.label: A
elimination.verdict: Innocence means absence of guilt or wrongdoing. It resembles insolence in spelling but is not its antonym.

elimination.label: B
elimination.verdict: Respect is the direct opposite of insolence. Correct.

elimination.label: C
elimination.verdict: Solace means comfort during distress; it has no semantic opposition to insolence.

elimination.label: D
elimination.verdict: Wealth concerns material resources and is unrelated to the relationship.

2026-1.shortcut: Name the relationship before reading the choices: antonym on the left means antonym on the right. Then use definitions, not sound or spelling.

pattern.immediate: Classify A-to-B as synonym, antonym, intensity, part-whole, function, or cause-effect.
pattern.shortcut: Apply that exact relationship and direction to C; reject phonetic look-alikes.

mistakes: Choosing innocence because it looks and sounds similar to insolence.
Finding a word related to insolence without preserving the antonym relationship.
Reversing the direction and looking for a synonym of insolence.
Using vague familiarity instead of stating each word's meaning.
sanity: Can both completed pairs be described by the same single word: antonyms?
Does the chosen word oppose insolence rather than merely sound similar?
The question asks for one option, so only one exact semantic match should remain.

cheat.rule: Identify the relation in the known pair before examining the missing pair.
cheat.trap: Spelling similarity is not semantic similarity.

2024-8.title: Mutual Funds and Weighted Return
2024-8.intuition: Both people invest the same total amount, Rs 50,000. Therefore the difference in their final amounts cannot come from principal; it comes only from how the common principal is distributed across funds with different return rates. Comparing allocation differences avoids two long final-balance equations and exposes one linear equation immediately.

examApproach.heading: Confirm that the principal cancels
examApproach.body: Each person invests Rs 50,000, so compare returns only.

examApproach.heading: Use allocation differences
examApproach.body: Person 1 has Rs 5,000 extra in B and C, but Rs 10,000 less in A. Let A's rate be r.

steps.heading: Compute both total investments
steps.body: Person 1 and Person 2 each invest Rs 50,000. The common principal contributes equally to their final amounts and cancels in a comparison.

steps.heading: Write Person 1's allocation relative to Person 2
steps.body: Person 1 invests Rs 10,000 less in A, Rs 5,000 more in B, and Rs 5,000 more in C.

steps.heading: Calculate the known advantage from B and C
steps.body: Both known funds return 15 percent.

steps.heading: Account for the lower investment in A
steps.body: If A returns rate r, Person 1 earns Rs 10,000r less from A than Person 2. His net advantage is given as Rs 500.

steps.heading: Solve and convert to a percentage

elimination.label: A
elimination.verdict: At 7.5 percent, the net advantage is Rs 1500 - Rs 750 = Rs 750, not Rs 500.

elimination.label: B
elimination.verdict: At 10 percent, the net advantage is Rs 1500 - Rs 1000 = Rs 500. Correct.

elimination.label: C
elimination.verdict: At 15 percent, all three funds return the same rate, so equal total investments give zero difference.

elimination.label: D
elimination.verdict: At 20 percent, Person 1 is behind by Rs 500 because Person 2 has more money in the higher-return fund A.

2024-8.shortcut: When total investments are equal, calculate only sum of allocation difference times return rate. Do not calculate two full maturity values.

pattern.trigger: Equal total principal but different allocations
pattern.immediate: The principal cancels; compare returns using signed allocation differences.
pattern.shortcut: Write one difference equation instead of two balance equations.

mistakes: Writing two complete final-balance equations and losing time.
Using 15 instead of 0.15 for a 15 percent return.
Forgetting that Person 1 has less, not more, invested in A; its contribution must be negative.
Comparing only the Rs 5,000 differences in B and C and ignoring fund A.
sanity: If A also returned 15 percent, equal total principal would force equal final amounts.
Because Person 1 still finishes ahead, A must return less than 15 percent; 10 percent is plausible.
Substituting 10 percent must reproduce exactly Rs 500.

cheat.rule: Compare signed allocation differences; common principal cancels.
cheat.trap: Keep the sign of each allocation difference.

2024-58.title: Bayes Rule with Complementary Cases
2024-58.intuition: The question gives how likely S is under T and under not-T, but asks for T after observing S. That is the reverse conditional, so Bayes' rule is required. The denominator must include every way in which S can occur: through T and through its complement.

examApproach.heading: Use two branches to find P(S)

steps.heading: Write the prior probabilities
steps.body: T and its complement partition the sample space.

steps.heading: Find the joint probability of T and S
steps.body: The path T followed by S has probability prior times likelihood.

steps.heading: Find the competing route to S
steps.body: S can also occur when T does not occur.

steps.heading: Compute the total evidence probability
steps.body: The two routes are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

2024-58.shortcut: Imagine 100 cases: 40 belong to T and 12 of them produce S; 60 belong to not-T and 36 produce S. Of the 48 total S cases, 12 came from T, so the answer is 12/48 = 0.25.

pattern.trigger: Asked for P(cause | evidence), given P(evidence | cause)
pattern.immediate: Reverse conditional means Bayes; build every route to the evidence.
pattern.shortcut: Use a 100-case frequency table when all probabilities have simple decimals.
pattern.formula: P(T\mid S)=\frac{P(S\mid T)P(T)}{P(S\mid T)P(T)+P(S\mid\overline T)P(\overline T)}

mistakes: Reporting P(S|T)=0.3 as the answer, which reverses the conditioning incorrectly.
Using only 0.12 in the denominator and forgetting S cases from not-T.
Using P(T)=0.6 instead of taking the complement to obtain 0.4.
Rounding intermediate values too early.
sanity: The result must lie between 0 and 1.
S is twice as likely under not-T as under T, so observing S should reduce belief in T below its prior 0.4; 0.25 does.
The two S branches must sum to 0.48 before normalization.

cheat.rule: Target joint probability divided by total probability of the evidence.
cheat.trap: The denominator includes every mutually exclusive route to the evidence.

2026-64.title: Dependent Row and Column Sums in a Bernoulli Matrix
testing: Conditioning on a shared Bernoulli variable
Dependence created by an overlapping matrix cell
2026-64.intuition: The second row and third column are not independent because they share the cell A_{2,3}. Condition on whether this common cell is 1 or 0. After fixing it, the remaining four row cells and four column cells are disjoint independent groups, so ordinary binomial probabilities apply.

examApproach.heading: Name the shared cell
examApproach.body: Let Z=A_{2,3}. Split the probability into Z=1 and Z=0 cases.

examApproach.heading: Count required ones in each case
examApproach.body: If Z=1, each remaining group of four needs 2 ones. If Z=0, each group needs 3 ones.

steps.heading: Identify why direct multiplication fails
steps.body: The row-sum event and column-sum event both depend on A_{2,3}; therefore they are not independent.

steps.heading: Condition on A_{2,3}=1
steps.body: The shared cell already contributes one to each sum. Each of the two disjoint groups of four remaining cells must contain exactly two ones.

steps.heading: Condition on A_{2,3}=0
steps.body: The shared cell contributes zero, so each remaining group of four must contain exactly three ones.

steps.heading: Round as requested
steps.body: Rounded to two decimal places, 0.1015625 becomes 0.10.

2026-64.shortcut: Whenever a row event and column event overlap in one cell, condition on that cell. This turns the remaining cells into two independent binomial groups.

pattern.trigger: Two counts share exactly one Bernoulli trial
pattern.immediate: They are dependent; condition on the shared trial.
pattern.shortcut: Split into shared value 0 and 1, multiply within each conditional branch, then add.

mistakes: Multiplying two Binomial(5,1/2) probabilities as though the row and column were independent.
Counting the shared cell twice.
If the shared cell is 1, asking the remaining four cells for three additional ones instead of two.
Reporting 0.1015625 without applying the requested two-decimal rounding.
sanity: The answer should be close to, but not exactly, the naive independent value [C(5,3)/32]^2.
The Z=1 and Z=0 cases are disjoint and cover all possibilities.
The exact probability 13/128 lies between 0 and 1 and rounds to 0.10.

cheat.rule: Condition on the intersection cell before using binomial probabilities.

2024-13.title: Classifying Eigenvalues of a Real 2 by 2 Matrix
testing: Characteristic polynomial from trace and determinant
Complex-conjugate eigenvalues of a real matrix
2024-13.intuition: The options ask only for the type of eigenvalues, so eigenvectors are unnecessary. For a real 2 by 2 matrix, compute trace and determinant, write the characteristic quadratic, and inspect its discriminant. A negative discriminant means the two eigenvalues are non-real complex conjugates.

examApproach.heading: Classify without finding eigenvectors
examApproach.body: A negative discriminant for a real quadratic gives a complex-conjugate pair, so option (B) is correct.

steps.heading: Write the matrix and characteristic determinant
Expand carefully
steps.body: The off-diagonal product is (-1)(3)=-3, and subtracting it adds 3.

steps.heading: Interpret the sign
steps.body: Since the coefficients are real and Delta is negative, the roots are non-real and occur as a conjugate pair.

steps.heading: Find the roots as a verification

elimination.label: A
elimination.verdict: False. The negative discriminant rules out real eigenvalues.

elimination.label: B
elimination.verdict: Correct. The roots are (3 plus/minus i sqrt(11))/2.

elimination.label: C
elimination.verdict: False. Zero would be an eigenvalue only if det(M)=0, but det(M)=5.

elimination.label: D
elimination.verdict: False. A positive and a negative real eigenvalue would give a negative determinant; here the determinant is positive and the roots are non-real.

2024-13.shortcut: For a real 2 by 2 matrix, use Delta=(trace)^2-4det. Its sign classifies the eigenvalues immediately.

pattern.trigger: Question asks real/complex type of 2 by 2 eigenvalues
pattern.immediate: Use trace, determinant, and the quadratic discriminant.
pattern.shortcut: Do not compute eigenvectors or diagonalize the matrix.

mistakes: Assuming every real matrix has real eigenvalues; only special classes such as real symmetric matrices guarantee that.
Computing det(M) as 2-3=-1 instead of 2-(-3)=5.
Using det(A-lambda I) with a sign error in the off-diagonal product.
Trying to infer signs from diagonal entries alone.
sanity: The two roots should sum to trace(M)=3.
Their product should equal det(M)=5.
A nonzero determinant immediately eliminates the option containing a zero eigenvalue.

cheat.trigger: Eigenvalue type for a real 2 by 2 matrix
cheat.rule: Classify roots with the characteristic discriminant.
cheat.trap: A real nonsymmetric matrix can have complex eigenvalues.

2024-13.final: (B) The eigenvalues form a complex-conjugate pair

2025-28.title: Spectrum of Identity plus a Rank-One Projector
testing: Eigenvalues of the outer product xx^T
Effect of adding the identity matrix
2025-28.intuition: Because x is a unit vector, xx^T is the orthogonal projector onto span{x}. It acts as 1 along x and as 0 on every vector perpendicular to x. Adding I shifts those eigenvalues to 2 and 1, so every eigenvalue of A is positive.

examApproach.heading: Split the space into two invariant parts
examApproach.body: Use span{x} and its orthogonal complement.

examApproach.heading: Answer all four options from the spectrum
examApproach.body: The spectrum is {2,1,...,1}; hence rank n and invertibility are true, while zero and negative inverse eigenvalues are impossible.

steps.heading: Evaluate xx^T along x
steps.body: The condition x^T x=1 makes x an eigenvector of xx^T with eigenvalue 1.

steps.heading: Evaluate xx^T on the orthogonal complement
steps.body: For any v with x^Tv=0, the outer product kills v.

steps.heading: Write the complete spectrum
steps.body: There is one eigenvalue 2 and n-1 eigenvalues 1.

steps.heading: Infer rank and inverse spectrum
steps.body: No eigenvalue is zero, so rank(A)=n and A is invertible. The eigenvalues of A^{-1} are reciprocals: 1/2 and 1, both positive.

elimination.label: A
elimination.verdict: True. Every eigenvalue is nonzero, so rank(A)=n.

elimination.label: B
elimination.verdict: True. A full-rank square matrix is invertible.

elimination.label: C
elimination.verdict: False. The smallest eigenvalue is 1, not 0.

elimination.label: D
elimination.verdict: False. A^{-1} has eigenvalues 1/2 and 1, so none is negative.

2025-28.shortcut: Recognize xx^T as a rank-one projector when x is unit. Adding I shifts its eigenvalues from {1,0} to {2,1}.

pattern.trigger: Matrix I plus/minus a unit-vector outer product
pattern.immediate: Decompose into the vector direction and its orthogonal complement.
pattern.shortcut: Read the two eigen-actions directly instead of computing a determinant.

mistakes: Concluding rank(A)=1 because xx^T has rank 1; adding I changes the full spectrum.
Forgetting the unit condition x^T x=1.
Assuming a rank-one update introduces a zero eigenvalue.
Thinking inverse eigenvalues are negatives rather than reciprocals.
sanity: A=I+xx^T is positive definite because z^TAz=||z||^2+(x^Tz)^2>0 for z nonzero.
The determinant is the product of eigenvalues, det(A)=2, so A must be invertible.
An inverse of a positive-definite matrix must also have positive eigenvalues.

cheat.rule: Use x and x-perpendicular subspaces; the eigenvalues are 2 and 1.
cheat.trap: Do not carry the rank-one rank over to I+xx^T.

2025-47.title: Tracing Python Set Operations with Simultaneous Assignment
2025-47.intuition: The decisive language rule is that every right-hand expression in A,B,C=... is evaluated using the old sets before any of the three names is rebound. Build one state table per executed if block. Reading the assignment left-to-right produces the wrong result.

examApproach.heading: Write only membership-relevant state
examApproach.body: Track complete A, B, and C after each simultaneous assignment; the loop continues only while other belongs to C.

examApproach.heading: Evaluate each right-hand side from the same old row
examApproach.body: For A,B,C=A-B,B-C,C-A, do not let the new A affect C-A.

examApproach.heading: Stop immediately when other leaves C
examApproach.body: After two iterations the final state is A={other}, B={this}, C={that}; therefore this occurs only in B.

steps.heading: Iteration 1 - first if block
steps.body: other is in C and this is in A, so evaluate all three differences from A_0,B_0,C_0.

steps.heading: Iteration 1 - second if block
steps.body: that is in B_1, so evaluate all three unions from the same A_1,B_1,C_1.

steps.heading: Iteration 2 - first if block
steps.body: other is still in C_2 and this is in A_2.

steps.heading: Terminate and inspect membership
steps.body: The second if is skipped because that is not in B_3. The while condition now fails because other is not in C_3. Only B_3 contains this.

elimination.label: A
elimination.verdict: False. Final A is {other}; it does not contain this.

elimination.label: B
elimination.verdict: Correct. Final B is {this}.

elimination.label: C
elimination.verdict: False. Final C is {that}.

elimination.label: D
elimination.verdict: False. this is not in final A or C.

2025-47.shortcut: Use a three-column trace table. Every comma-separated assignment creates the next row from the previous row, never from partially updated values.

pattern.trigger: Python multiple assignment with mutable collections
pattern.immediate: All right-hand sides use the pre-assignment state.
pattern.shortcut: Write old state, calculate every RHS, then write the new state.

mistakes: Updating A first and then using that new A while calculating B or C.
Reversing set difference: A-B is not B-A.
Testing the second if against the old B instead of the B produced by the first if.
Forgetting to re-check the while condition after the second iteration.
sanity: Each set operation result must contain only elements already present in the operands.
At termination, other must not be in C.
Check membership in the final sets, not in an intermediate iteration.

cheat.rule: Evaluate the full right-hand tuple first, then rebind all left-hand names.
cheat.trap: Never trace simultaneous assignment as sequential assignment.

2026-58.title: Recursive Bubble Pass and Total Swap Count
testing: Tracing recursive mutation of a list
Inversion count as total adjacent swaps
2026-58.intuition: One call to fun scans adjacent pairs from left to right and returns the number of swaps in that pass. The outer loop calls it five times, so the list becomes sorted after repeated bubble passes. You can trace every pass, then verify the total with the inversion-count theorem: adjacent-swap sorting performs exactly one swap per initial inversion.

examApproach.heading: Recognize the code pattern
examApproach.body: The recursion increments i after comparing L[i] and L[i+1], so one call is one bubble pass.

examApproach.heading: Verify with inversions
examApproach.body: The initial list has 4+2+2=8 inversions, confirming the trace.

steps.heading: Pass 1
steps.body: Starting from [5,3,4,1,2], 5 swaps successively with 3, 4, 1, and 2.

steps.heading: Pass 2
steps.body: The first pair is ordered. Then 4 swaps with 1 and with 2.

steps.heading: Pass 3
steps.body: 3 swaps with 1 and then with 2.

steps.heading: Passes 4 and 5
steps.body: The list is already sorted, so both calls return 0 and do not mutate the list.

steps.heading: Independent inversion check
steps.body: In [5,3,4,1,2], 5 forms four inversions; 3 forms two with 1 and 2; 4 forms two with 1 and 2.

2026-58.shortcut: Count inversions instead of tracing every recursive comparison: each adjacent swap removes exactly one inversion, so the total swaps required to sort equals the initial inversion count.

pattern.immediate: Bubble behavior; total swaps equal inversion count.
pattern.shortcut: Count, for each element, how many later elements are smaller.

mistakes: Counting five outer iterations as five swaps.
Forgetting that fun mutates data, so the next outer iteration sees the updated list.
Counting comparisons rather than only executions of the swap branch.
Stopping after the first pass when the list is not yet sorted.
sanity: The final list after all passes must be [1,2,3,4,5].
The accumulated count cannot exceed the maximum 5*4/2=10 inversions for five elements.
The traced total and independent inversion count should agree.

cheat.rule: Total successful adjacent swaps equal the initial inversion count.
cheat.trap: Pass count, comparison count, and swap count are different quantities.

2024-43.title: Collapsing a Positive-Input ReLU Network
testing: When ReLU behaves as the identity
Path-product expansion of a feed-forward network
Counting parallel paths from each input
2024-43.intuition: Every input is positive, every displayed weight in Figure 1 is positive, and all biases are zero. Therefore every hidden preactivation is positive and each ReLU passes its input unchanged. The network is linear on this input region, so the coefficient of each x_i is the sum of the weight products over every directed path from x_i to the output.

examApproach.heading: Remove ReLU after checking signs
examApproach.body: Positive inputs times positive weights with zero biases keep every hidden unit active.

examApproach.heading: Find gain per complete path
examApproach.body: Every path uses weights 1, then 2, then 3.

examApproach.heading: Count paths
examApproach.body: x1 has 3*2=6 paths; x2 and x3 each have 2*2=4 paths. Multiply by gain 6 to obtain p=36, q=24, r=24.

steps.heading: Establish the active ReLU region
steps.body: For x1,x2,x3>0, each first-layer unit receives a positive weighted sum. The same remains true in later layers because their incoming weights are 2 and 3. Thus ReLU(z)=z at every neuron.

steps.heading: Compute one path's multiplicative gain
steps.body: A complete path crosses an input-to-first-layer edge of weight 1, a first-to-second-layer edge of weight 2, and a second-layer-to-output edge of weight 3.

steps.heading: Count paths from x1
steps.body: Figure 1 connects x1 to all three first-layer nodes. Every one of those nodes connects to both second-layer nodes.

steps.heading: Count paths from x2
steps.body: The figure gives x2 two first-layer connections; each continues to two second-layer nodes.

steps.heading: Count paths from x3
steps.body: x3 has the same connection count as x2.

elimination.label: A
elimination.verdict: Matches the path counts: p=36, q=24, r=24. Correct.

elimination.label: B
elimination.verdict: Swaps the larger x1 coefficient with x3; Figure 1 gives x1 more outgoing paths.

elimination.label: C
elimination.verdict: The coefficients do not match either the common path gain 6 or the path multiplicities.

elimination.label: D
elimination.verdict: Would require x2 and x3 to have as many paths as x1, which the figure does not show.

2024-43.shortcut: Once all ReLUs are guaranteed active, treat the network as linear. Coefficient of an input equals sum over paths of product of edge weights.

pattern.trigger: ReLU network with guaranteed positive preactivations
pattern.immediate: All ReLUs are identity on this region.
pattern.shortcut: Count paths and multiply edge weights instead of expanding neuron equations one layer at a time.

mistakes: Removing ReLU without first checking that every preactivation is positive.
Multiplying one representative path but forgetting to add parallel paths.
Counting first-layer connections only and forgetting that each branches to two second-layer nodes.
Assuming every input has the same coefficient despite different connectivity.
sanity: All effective coefficients must be positive.
x2 and x3 have symmetric connectivity in the figure, so q must equal r.
x1 has more paths than x2 or x3, so p must be larger than q and r.

cheat.rule: ReLU becomes identity; sum path-weight products.

2025-57.title: Candidate Keys and BCNF from Attribute Closures
2025-57.intuition: Candidate keys require both completeness and minimality. First compute closures of likely determinants. Then check BCNF separately: every nontrivial functional dependency must have a superkey on its left side. A relation can have correctly identified candidate keys and still violate BCNF because of one non-key determinant.

examApproach.heading: Compute A+ and (BC)+
examApproach.body: A reaches BCEF, then E reaches DG, so A reaches all attributes. BC reaches A and therefore all attributes.

examApproach.heading: Rule out E as a key
examApproach.body: E+={E,D,G}; it cannot reach A, B, C, or F.

examApproach.heading: Check BCNF determinants
examApproach.body: A and BC are superkeys, but E is not. Hence E->DG violates BCNF.

steps.heading: Compute A closure
steps.body: Start with A. Apply A->BCEF, then use the newly obtained E in E->DG.

steps.heading: Check minimality of A
steps.body: A is a single attribute and its closure is all of R, so it is automatically a minimal superkey: a candidate key.

steps.heading: Compute BC closure
steps.body: BC first determines A; then A and E activate the remaining dependencies.

steps.heading: Check minimality of BC
steps.body: B+={B} and C+={C}; neither alone is a superkey. Therefore BC is a candidate key.

steps.heading: Show there are no other candidate keys
steps.body: The only dependency that produces A is BC->A. Any key without A must therefore contain both B and C, whose minimal version is BC. Any key containing A has the smaller key A. Thus the only candidate keys are A and BC.

steps.heading: Test BCNF
steps.body: A->BCEF and BC->A have superkey determinants. But E is not a superkey because E+={E,D,G}; therefore the nontrivial dependency E->DG violates BCNF.

elimination.label: A
elimination.verdict: False. BC is also a minimal key.

elimination.label: B
elimination.verdict: True. The only candidate keys are A and BC.

elimination.label: C
elimination.verdict: False. E+={E,D,G}, so E is not a key.

elimination.label: D
elimination.verdict: True. E->DG has a determinant E that is not a superkey, violating BCNF.

2025-57.shortcut: Find closures of FD left sides first. For BCNF, stop as soon as a nontrivial FD has a determinant whose closure is not all attributes.

pattern.immediate: Use closure for keys; then separately test every FD determinant for BCNF.
pattern.shortcut: A non-superkey determinant proves BCNF violation immediately.

mistakes: Calling every superkey a candidate key without checking minimality.
Calling E a key because it determines D and G, while ignoring A, B, C, and F.
Checking BCNF only for dependencies whose left sides are candidate keys and overlooking E->DG.
Assuming that having candidate keys A and BC automatically makes the relation BCNF.
sanity: Every claimed key must derive F; E cannot, so E cannot be a key.
Removing B or C from BC must destroy the superkey property.
One BCNF violation is enough; there is no need to decompose the relation because the question asks only whether it is in BCNF.

cheat.trigger: FDs with candidate-key and BCNF options
cheat.rule: Compute closures, enforce minimality, then test whether each determinant is a superkey.
cheat.formula: X\text{ is a key if }X^+=R\text{ and no proper subset has closure }R
cheat.trap: Candidate-key discovery and BCNF validation are separate checks.
